intro: The Christopher C. Kraft, Jr. Mission Control Center in Houston monitors the ISS around the clock and oversees Artemis lunar round-trips. Flight makes the decisions, CAPCOM becomes the crew's only voice, and each console guards its own system.
lessons.0.title: Mission Control Is Not an Unmanned Spacecraft
lessons.0.summary: The control room is an extension of the spacecraft. People on the ground allocate the time, safety, and science of the humans in orbit.
lessons.0.body.0: The Christopher C. Kraft, Jr. Mission Control Center at Johnson Space Center is the hub for human spaceflight. Official descriptions state that this facility handles flight planning, crew training, flight product generation, and real-time operations support, monitoring the ISS and its inhabitants on a 24/7 basis. Beyond low Earth orbit, Artemis lunar round-trips also fall under this same control responsibility.
lessons.0.body.1: During the course, candidates shift into the Houston control room to experience a day in the life of the people who watch over astronauts and spacecraft. This is an observation to prepare them for the day they may find themselves on the other side of the loop, receiving instructions.
lessons.0.body.2: Control is not a place that issues commands from above. Each console knows the limits of its system, Flight integrates them, and CAPCOM conveys them to the crew. In comprehensive exercises, we observe whether these three layers function simultaneously.
lessons.0.facts.0.label: Official Name
lessons.0.facts.1.label: Monitoring
lessons.0.deepDive.title: Control Is a Combination of Specialized Division and Integrated Judgment
lessons.0.deepDive.body.0: A single anomaly can ripple across multiple systems. Considering a situation where a power issue affects thermal control or life support, it becomes clear why simply assigning the issue to a responsible console is not enough. A role is also needed to synthesize specialized analyses and determine overall priorities.
lessons.0.deepDive.body.1: In this exercise, you first select one responsible console to consult. In reality, multiple consoles and support teams coordinate. To make it easier for the next person in charge to continue making judgments, organize the information you hand off in this order: observed state, actions taken, results, and unresolved points.
lessons.1.title: The Layout of the FCR Is the Flow of Information
lessons.1.summary: Whether in the White Room or an ISS room, Flight is placed in the center, with system consoles seated within reach of sight and voice.
lessons.1.body.0: MCC has multiple Flight Control Rooms (FCRs). Official explanations of Artemis I list FCR-1, FCR-2, and the Red / White / Blue FCRs, describing the White FCR as a result of the MCC-21 renovation for 21st-century deep space flight. The White FCR is positioned as the room responsible for Orion deep space missions.
lessons.1.body.1: The daily routine of the ISS operates in a different FCR (official photos record FCR-1 as being used for the ISS). The large screen on the front wall creates a shared reality for everyone regarding orbit, attitude, and the next event. The short names of each console serve as signs that indicate in one second who is watching which system.
lessons.1.body.2: The quietness of the room does not mean idleness. Only necessary voices enter the loop. Small talk is pushed to the back room, leaving only decisions and confirmations in the front room. When candidates visit, the first thing they should learn is not the seating chart, but which voices move the room.
lessons.1.facts.0.label: ISS Routine
lessons.1.facts.1.label: Deep Space
lessons.2.title: Flight Is the Conductor of the Orchestra
lessons.2.summary: The Flight Director oversees all consoles and support rooms, holding responsibility for execution from ignition to post-splashdown power-down.
lessons.2.body.0: Official role descriptions call Flight the "maestro of the orchestra," supervising all controllers in the control and support rooms. Explanations of Artemis I state that Flight is responsible for execution, commands, and troubleshooting from SLS ignition to the power-down after Orion splashdown and handover to the recovery team. The seat is placed near the center of the room, optimized for coordination with other consoles.
lessons.2.body.1: In an official episode of Houston We Have a Podcast, an active Flight Director defines the role as "leading the team to make real-time decisions." As an example of a career path, the route from the Trajectory and Orbital Planning Office (TOPO) to the front room is discussed. Integration is impossible without depth in a specific system.
lessons.2.body.2: In Flight terminology, the room moves. "GO," "NO-GO," "Stand by," "I need a recommendation." The job is to distill the limit values gathered from the consoles into a single sentence, not to rely on individual intuition. Silence is not approval. It is also Flight's decision whether to wait until the required consoles are ready or to proceed without them.
lessons.2.facts.0.label: Position
lessons.2.facts.0.value: Near the center of the room
lessons.2.facts.1.label: Responsibility
lessons.3.title: CAPCOM is the team's single voice and the crew's advocate
lessons.3.summary: In principle, only one person speaks to the spacecraft. Ground expertise is compressed into a single sentence that the crew can use right now.
lessons.3.body.0: Official explanations define CAPCOM (capsule communicator) as the person who speaks with astronauts. In a podcast, an active CAPCOM described the role as the "single voice from the team to the crew" and simultaneously the "advocate for the crew in the control room." It is not just about giving instructions; it is about bringing the crew's perspective back to the room.
lessons.3.body.1: When multiple consoles want to speak at the same time, feeding everything into the loop would cause the crew to stop working. CAPCOM prioritizes, separating the procedure to do now from information that can wait. Official sources also highlight examples of individuals maintaining CAPCOM qualifications while serving as Station Utilization Integrators, connecting the constraints of scientific research and the crew's daily schedule through a single voice.
lessons.3.body.2: Historically, CAPCOMs were often astronauts. Current official explanations indicate that experienced controllers and engineers also hold this position. The essence of the qualification is not the title, but the ability to imagine the crew's workload.
lessons.3.facts.0.label: Principle
lessons.3.facts.1.label: Another aspect
lessons.3.facts.1.value: Advocacy for the crew in the room
lessons.4.title: Each console advocates for the limits of its system
lessons.4.summary: Consoles with abbreviated names monitor power, environment, orbit, communications, and activity plans simultaneously. Integrated exercises are training for this distribution of responsibilities.
lessons.4.body.0: Explanations of Artemis I state that each console represents its system with an abbreviated title, sharing the load of rocket and spacecraft subsystems. On the ISS side as well, qualified controllers sit for each system, such as attitude, power, thermal control, communications, orbit, extravehicular activity, and utilization (science).
lessons.4.body.1: An anomaly cannot be closed by a single console. A power drop simultaneously affects thermal control, communications, and the experiment schedule. Therefore, each console states in numbers "how far its system can hold," and Flight makes the trade-off. The mini-game in integrated exercises exists to teach why anomalies must be routed to the correct console.
lessons.4.body.2: The back room (support room) digs up the materials the front room uses for decisions. When the front room is silent, procedures and telemetry are moving behind the scenes. Candidates experience MCC shifts to feel this dual structure firsthand.
lessons.4.facts.0.label: Front
lessons.4.facts.1.label: Back
lessons.5.title: Loops and screens create a shared reality
lessons.5.summary: Audio loops and front-wall screens align who knows what. Speaking as if one knows, without verification, leads to accidents.
lessons.5.body.0: Controllers listen to multiple audio loops simultaneously: their own system, Flight, CAPCOM, and adjacent consoles. They press the transmit key only when necessary, keeping call signs and content short. Official operational culture treats this brevity as a safety device.
lessons.5.body.1: Front-wall screens show everyone the orbit, next LOS/AOS, attitude, and major events. Console details remain with the individual, while the room's shared reality is placed on the screens. Explanations to the crew must also use words that do not contradict this shared reality.
lessons.5.body.2: Communication dropouts are routine. Whether on the ISS or near the Moon, there are times when line-of-sight and relay are cut. Before the cut, one must hand over "what to do next and when to call back." Upon return, do not fill gaps with speculation; re-synchronize reality with telemetry.
lessons.5.facts.0.label: Audio
lessons.5.facts.1.label: Visual
lessons.6.title: GO/NO-GO is not a vote, but a declaration of limits
lessons.6.summary: Each console answers not "do we want to go," but "is my system within acceptable limits." Flight turns this collection into a decision.
lessons.6.body.0: Before launch, rendezvous, extravehicular activity, and reentry, Flight calls the consoles in order. The answer is not a matter of mood. Fuel, power, attitude, communications, weather, crew health. If any one exceeds its limit, it is NO-GO, and that console must provide the reason and recovery conditions.
lessons.6.body.1: The explanation of Artemis I states that Kennedy Launch Control is responsible for the countdown, and after liftoff, Houston's MCC takes over the flight until splashdown. Even though the location changes, the logic of a GO remains the same. At the moment of handover, do not leave it ambiguous who holds execution responsibility.
lessons.6.body.2: In training, values near the boundaries are intentionally produced to see if a NO-GO can be called. A room that cannot call a NO-GO will later be forced into worse choices. Astronauts also return their physical condition and procedure progress to CAPCOM without hiding anything.
lessons.6.facts.0.label: Meaning
lessons.6.facts.1.label: Handover
lessons.7.title: Integrated Simulation Builds Qualification
lessons.7.summary: SimSup throws anomalies, and the room responds with procedures and priorities. The calm of the real thing stands on thousands of failures.
lessons.7.body.0: Before crewed flight, the crew and control repeat integrated simulations. Official candidate courses also list diverse simulations using Johnson facilities, virtual reality, and immersive technologies. A room's qualification is not enough with individual subject exams alone.
lessons.7.body.1: In simulations, fire, depressurization, power loss, communication loss, and rendezvous delays overlap. Switch to the correct console, CAPCOM crafts a single sentence to pass to the crew, and Flight cuts it: 'Life first, then the ship, then the mission.' Internalizing this priority is the purpose of comprehensive exercises.
lessons.7.body.2: A failed simulation is not a shame. In the debrief, verbalize which information was delayed and which loop was crossed. If the same anomaly occurs in the real thing, the room will not show a first-time face.
lessons.7.facts.0.label: Goal
lessons.7.facts.1.label: Evaluation
lessons.8.title: Crew and Ground Speak Assuming They Cannot See Each Other
lessons.8.summary: In orbit, the perception of sound and smell is different. Ground wins in telemetry resolution. Only by adding both do you get the situation.
lessons.8.body.0: The official self-definition of CAPCOM is to support the crew's day, pass necessary tasks, and simultaneously expand the crew's perspective to the room. Ground wins in sensor resolution, but the feel of vibration, smell, and the inability to open a procedure manual page is held only by the crew.
lessons.8.body.1: Therefore, do not end reports with 'It is normal.' Add a word explaining the basis for normality. Conversely, ground does not flood the crew with raw numbers. Compress it into a single sentence that affects the current operation.
lessons.8.body.2: Candidates experience control shifts to see what their future omitted reports will break in the room. In comprehensive exercises, that omission is intentionally triggered to measure who notices.
lessons.8.facts.0.label: Ground Strength
lessons.8.facts.1.label: Onboard Strength
lessons.9.title: In Compound Anomalies, Cut in the Order of Life, Ship, Mission
lessons.9.summary: If you try to fix all alarms ringing at once, all will be delayed. Passing a comprehensive exercise means being able to state the order of what to discard.
lessons.9.body.0: ISS emergencies are represented by fire, rapid depressurization, and toxic atmosphere (such as ammonia). In lunar round trips, propulsion, power, heat, communication, and life support degrade over long delays. In any plan, the first thing to protect is the crew's life, next the spacecraft's controllability, and then the mission objectives.
lessons.9.body.1: Triage examples look simple. Smoke goes to Environment and Medical, power drop to Power and Thermal, orbital deviation to TOPO and Attitude. In reality, they come simultaneously. Flight designates 'who leads now,' and other consoles do not interfere with the lead but only raise limit values.
lessons.9.body.2: All courses so far—systems, medicine, EVA, robotics, flight, emergencies, geology—existed to be compressed into a single sentence in this room. Certification is not memorizing knowledge, but being able to state the correct console and correct order before time runs out.
lessons.9.facts.0.label: 1st
lessons.9.facts.1.label: 2nd / 3rd
quiz.0.prompt: Who is the person included in the official name of Houston's crewed flight control center?
quiz.0.choices.3: A name bearing only Gene Kranz
quiz.0.explanation: The official page calls Johnson's facility the Christopher C. Kraft, Jr. Mission Control Center.
quiz.1.prompt: Which combination does the official description list as MCC's monitoring targets?
quiz.1.choices.1: 24-hour monitoring of ISS and Artemis lunar round trips
quiz.1.choices.2: Reproduction of the Apollo program only
quiz.1.choices.3: Day shift of uncrewed Mars rovers only
quiz.1.explanation: It is officially stated that MCC monitors ISS and crew 24/7, and beyond low orbit, also supervises Artemis lunar round trips.
quiz.2.prompt: Which room does the Artemis I explanation list as modified for deep space Orion flights?
quiz.2.explanation: The White FCR, modified as MCC-21, is positioned as the control room responsible for Orion's deep space missions.
quiz.3.prompt: Which phrase is used in the official role description to metaphorically describe Flight?
quiz.3.explanation: JSC's MCC explanation describes the Flight Director as the maestro of an orchestra, overseeing all controllers.
quiz.4.prompt: Which is the correct scope of responsibility for Flight as indicated in the Artemis I explanation?
quiz.4.choices.0: From SLS ignition to power-down after Orion's splashdown and handover to the recovery team
quiz.4.choices.1: Only during the last 10 seconds of the countdown
quiz.4.choices.2: Only peer review of scientific papers
quiz.4.choices.3: Only welding inspection of the launch pad
quiz.4.explanation: It is stated that Flight holds execution responsibility from booster ignition through power-down after splashdown and handover to the recovery team.
quiz.5.prompt: Which is the official meaning of CAPCOM?
quiz.5.explanation: CAPCOM stands for capsule communicator, the position responsible for communicating with the astronauts.
quiz.6.prompt: What does an active CAPCOM identify as the two aspects of their role in the official podcast?
quiz.6.choices.2: Being the single voice from the team to the crew, and advocating for the crew in the room
quiz.6.explanation: Amy Dill states that CAPCOM is the single voice of the team and simultaneously the advocate for the crew in the control room.
quiz.7.prompt: In a complex anomaly, what should each console pass to Flight?
quiz.7.choices.1: Criticism of other consoles' work only
quiz.7.choices.3: The limit values indicating how far their system can currently hold
quiz.7.explanation: Each console represents the tolerances of their system in numbers and conditions, while Flight makes the integrated judgment.
quiz.8.prompt: What is the transfer of responsibility from launch to flight as indicated in the Artemis I explanation?
quiz.8.choices.0: Kennedy's launch control handles the countdown, and Houston's MCC takes over from ascent until splashdown
quiz.8.choices.2: The crew also handles ground control
quiz.8.choices.3: Switch to uncrewed operations after launch
quiz.8.explanation: It is officially organized that KSC performs the countdown, and MCC takes over the flight from ignition until splashdown.
quiz.9.prompt: What does the official article state regarding the MCC experience for candidates?
quiz.9.choices.0: Painting the walls of the control room
quiz.9.choices.1: Working a shift in Houston's control room and experiencing a day as an observer
quiz.9.explanation: The article 'Astronaut Candidates Get to Work' states that candidates work a shift in MCC and experience a day on the monitoring side.
quiz.10.prompt: What should ground and crew share before communication is lost?
quiz.10.choices.2: What to do next and when to call back
quiz.10.explanation: Before LOS, the next task and re-call time are passed; after return, resynchronization is done via telemetry, not guesswork.
quiz.11.prompt: What is the order of priority for cutting systems in a complex anomaly as indicated by this department?
quiz.11.explanation: Priorities are cut in the order of life, vehicle controllability, and mission objectives. Trying to fix everything at once delays everything.
quiz.12.prompt: In the official podcast, which group did a certain Flight Director say they belonged to before moving to the front room?
quiz.12.explanation: Garrett Hehn states that he started with TOPO (trajectory experts) and then moved to the flight console.
quiz.13.prompt: When multiple consoles speak to the crew simultaneously, what should CAPCOM do?
quiz.13.choices.0: Loop all consoles' statements to the crew simultaneously
quiz.13.choices.1: Prioritize information, separating immediate procedures from later information
quiz.13.choices.2: Remain silent and leave it to the crew
quiz.13.explanation: As the single voice, CAPCOM compresses information and delivers it in an order that does not stop the crew's work.
quiz.14.prompt: What is an appropriate primary purpose of integrated simulation?
quiz.14.choices.2: Synchronizing the crew and control rooms on anomaly priority and distribution
quiz.14.choices.3: Designing a new rocket on the spot
quiz.14.explanation: Integrated sims are conducted to route anomalies to the correct console and to embody CAPCOM's single voice and Flight's priorities throughout the room.
quiz.15.prompt: What should each console answer at the GO/NO-GO poll?
quiz.15.choices.3: Whether their system is within acceptable limits, and if NO, the conditions for recovery
quiz.15.explanation: The poll is not a vote of preference. Each console declares the limits of its system, and Flight turns the collective input into a decision.
glossary.0.description: The human flight control hub at Johnson Space Center. It monitors the ISS 24 hours a day and also oversees Artemis.
glossary.1.description: The front room where controllers are seated. There are separate rooms for ISS and deep space (such as the White FCR).
glossary.2.description: The commander who oversees all consoles and support rooms, responsible for real-time execution decisions and commands.
glossary.3.description: Theoretically the only voice speaking to the crew. It compresses ground expertise while simultaneously bringing the crew's perspective back to the room.
glossary.4.description: The group of orbital experts. In official interviews, they are also described as providing trajectory examples to Flight.
glossary.5.description: A confirmation where each console declares its system's acceptability, and Flight decides whether to proceed. It is not a vote of preference.
glossary.6.description: Audio channels organized by system and role. Transmissions occur only when necessary to prevent cross-talk in the room.
glossary.7.description: A group of specialists that provides material to the front FCR. They are responsible for digging into telemetry and procedures.
glossary.8.description: Training where the crew and control respond to anomalies simultaneously. Room qualifications are built here.
glossary.9.description: Loss of communication visibility or relay interruption. Before the signal cuts, the next task and re-call are handed off, and re-synchronization occurs upon return.
